## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$
([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $n\ge1$, let $H^{\otimes n}$ be the $n$-fold
completed tensor power with $H^{\otimes1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$, let $(U_\pi)_{\pi\in S_n}$
be the permutation unitaries and let
$P_\sigma^{(n)}$, $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$, be the sector projections
([[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]), with sector space
$$\mathfrak H_n^\sigma:=\operatorname{ran}P_\sigma^{(n)}\subseteq H^{\otimes n}.$$
For $O\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ let $O^{(i)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$
be the operator of clause (a) below, and put
$$\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^n O^{(i)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n}).$$
Identify $H^{\otimes n}$ with $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$ by the
surjective linear isometry $J_n$ of clause (b) below, and let
$\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}$ be the partial trace of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-finite-partial-trace-and-schmidt]] clause (a) over the
second factor of that identification. Then:

(a) *slot operators*: for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$ and every
$i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ there is a unique $O^{(i)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$
with $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i-1}\otimes Ov_i\otimes v_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$
for all $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$; it satisfies $\|O^{(i)}\|\le\|O\|$ and
$(O^*)^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$; in particular $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$;

(b) *parenthesisation*: the assignment
$v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$
extends to a surjective linear isometry
$J_n:H^{\otimes n}\to H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$;

(c) *permutation invariance*: $U_\pi\,\Sigma(O)\,U_\pi^*=\Sigma(O)$ for every
$\pi\in S_n$; consequently $\Sigma(O)$ preserves both sector spaces and commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$:
$$\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)};$$

(d) *trace law*: for every density operator $\rho$ on the sector space
$\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]
clause (a)), with zero extension $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$
obtained by regarding $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$, and
for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=n\,\operatorname{tr}(\gamma\,O)$,
where $\gamma:=J_n^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}(J_n\widetilde\rho\,J_n^{-1})\bigr)J_n$;

(e) *the reduced operator is a density operator*: the operator $\gamma$ of
clause (d) is a density operator on $H$; it is independent of the choice of
slot in the sense that it equals the partial trace of $\widetilde\rho$ over
the other $n-1$ slots in the parenthesisation in which the retained slot is
the one the display names;

(f) *scope*: clauses (a)-(e) are exact operator identities on the
finite-dimensional labelled tensor powers; no physical system, particle
species, preparation or measurement is asserted, and the parameter $n$ is a
dimension count of the construction, not an observed particle number.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $H$ of dimension $d\ge1$, the integer $n\ge1$, the completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$ with permutation unitaries $U_\pi$ and sector projections $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, the operator $O\in\mathcal B(H)$, the slot index $i$, and the density operator $\rho$ on $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ with its zero extension $\widetilde\rho$.

[F1] **Tensor powers.** $H^{\otimes n}$ is a complex Hilbert space; the elementary tensors have dense linear span; $\|v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\|=\|v_1\|\cdots\|v_n\|$ and $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_{k}\langle v_k,w_k\rangle$; for orthonormal families spanning $H$ the corresponding elementary tensors form an orthonormal family with dense span ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clauses (b), (c), (d)).

[F2] **Parenthesisation.** For every parenthesisation the iterated tensor product represents multilinear maps, and different parenthesisations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors ([[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]).

[F3] **Bounded tensor maps.** For $S,T\in\mathcal B(H)$ there is a unique $S\otimes T\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H)$ with $(S\otimes T)(u\otimes v)=Su\otimes Tv$, $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$, $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$, and for endomorphisms $S\otimes I$ and $I\otimes T$ commute ([[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] clauses (a), (b), (c)).

[F4] **Permutation unitaries and sectors.** $U_\pi$ is unitary with $U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$ and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$; $U_\pi P_+^{(n)}=P_+^{(n)}U_\pi=P_+^{(n)}$ and $U_\pi P_-^{(n)}=P_-^{(n)}U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-^{(n)}$; the range of $P_+^{(n)}$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-^{(n)}$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] clauses (a), (b), (c)).

[F5] **Partial trace.** For endomorphisms $R$ of $V\otimes W$ with $V,W$ finite-dimensional, there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A)=\operatorname{tr}(R(A\otimes I_W))$ for every $A\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, independent of the orthonormal basis used in its construction; if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$ ([[thm-nrqm-composites-finite-partial-trace-and-schmidt]] clauses (a), (b)).

[F6] **Density operators.** A density operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert space is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator of trace one ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a), [[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]).

[F7] **Trace laws.** The trace of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space is basis independent, linear, and $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]], [[prop-trace-is-linear]]); for a trace-class operator $T$ and bounded $S$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS)$ ([[thm-cyclicity-of-the-trace]]).

[F8] **Agreement on dense sets.** Two bounded linear operators from a normed space into a Banach space that agree on a dense subspace are equal ([[thm-extension-of-a-bounded-map-from-a-dense-subspace]]).

[F9] **Unitary conjugation preserves the operator norm.** If $U$ is unitary then $\|UTU^*\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; construct the slot operators by conjugating the first-slot tensor map with a permutation unitary, transport the partial trace through the parenthesisation isometry, and reduce every slot to the first by permutation invariance and cyclicity.

**Given:** the data of the statement and [F1]-[F9].

1.1 [The parenthesisation isometry] The map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]

1.2 [The first-slot operator] By [F3] the operator $O\otimes I_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)})$ is bounded with $(O\otimes I)(u\otimes w)=Ou\otimes w$. Transporting it through the isometry $J_n$ of clause (b) gives a bounded operator $A_1:=J_n^{-1}(O\otimes I)J_n$ on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $A_1(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=J_n^{-1}(Ov_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=Ov_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for all $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 [The zero extension and its symmetry] Regard $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and put $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$, an endomorphism of $H^{\otimes n}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is $\rho$ and which vanishes on the orthogonal complement; then $\widetilde\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F6] and [F7], so $\widetilde\rho$ is a density operator on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$. Since $U_\pi$ preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and acts on it as the scalar $\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)$ by [F4], $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 [Slot operators and the permutation invariance of their sum] Fix $i$, choose $\pi\in S_n$ with $\pi(1)=i$ and set $O^{(i)}:=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$; [F9] and step 1.2 give $\|O^{(i)}\|=\|O\otimes I\|\le\|O\|$, and [F3], [F4] give $(O^{(i)})^*=U_\pi(O^*\otimes I)U_\pi^*=(O^*)^{(i)}$, so $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$. On elementary tensors, [F4] gives $U_\pi^*(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi(n)}$; step 1.2 replaces the first factor by $Ov_{\pi(1)}=Ov_i$; and $U_\pi$ then moves that factor to slot $\pi(1)=i$, leaving every other factor in its original slot, so $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Ov_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$. If $\pi'$ is another permutation with $\pi'(1)=i$, then $\tau:=\pi^{-1}\pi'$ fixes $1$ and $U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*$ agrees with $A_1$ on elementary tensors by [F1], [F3], hence equals it by [F8]; thus $U_{\pi'}A_1U_{\pi'}^*=U_\pi U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*U_\pi^*=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*$ and $O^{(i)}$ is well defined, with the displayed elementary-tensor action. For $\tau\in S_n$ one then has $U_\tau O^{(i)}U_\tau^*=U_{\tau\pi}A_1U_{\tau\pi}^*=O^{(\tau(i))}$, and summing over $i$ with $\tau$ permuting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ gives $U_\tau\Sigma(O)U_\tau^*=\Sigma(O)$ for $\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^nO^{(i)}$; equivalently $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with every $U_\tau$. Since $P_\sigma^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)U_\pi$ is a finite linear combination of the $U_\pi$ by [F4], $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, so it preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and its orthogonal complement and $\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}$; this proves (a) and (c). [F1, F3, F4, F8, F9, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 [Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] Fix $i$ and $\pi$ with $\pi(1)=i$; by steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*)=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$, where the middle equality is cyclicity and the last uses $U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi=\widetilde\rho$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}((O\otimes I)J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})=n\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})O)$ by [F7], [F5] and the explicit form of $A_1$ in step 1.2; with the definition of $\gamma$ this is (d). By [F5] clause (b) applied with $R=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, which is positive of trace one by step 1.3, the operator $\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$ is positive of trace one, so its conjugate $\gamma$ is a density operator on $H$. If instead another named slot is retained, the same computation with the corresponding slot operator produces $\gamma'$ with $n\operatorname{tr}((\gamma'-\gamma)O)=0$ for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$, hence $\gamma'=\gamma$ on testing against the rank-one operators $O=T_{u,v}$, for which $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]); this proves (e) as well. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 [Conclusion and scope] Step 1.1 proves (b), step 2.1 proves (a) and (c), and step 3.1 proves (d) and (e); every argument used only the finite-dimensional tensor construction, the permutation sectors, the partial trace and the trace axioms, and no physical object, preparation or measurement entered, which is clause (f). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Reading of the identities.** The law $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=n\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)$ says that the mean of the sum of one-body slot operators in the sector preparation is $n$ times the trace pairing of a single one-particle operator with a reduced operator $\gamma$ on the one-particle space. Only the identity is asserted here; its physical reading requires the framework postulates and a declared preparation, and is stated separately.
- **Why the factor $n$ appears.** The sum $\Sigma(O)$ has $n$ slot terms with equal pairings by permutation invariance of the sector state, and $\gamma$ is normalised once, $\operatorname{tr}\gamma=1$; the factor $n$ is the multiplicity of the sum, not a further normalisation.

On elementary tensors, [F4] gives $U_\pi^*(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi(n)}$; step 1.2 replaces the first factor by $Ov_{\pi(1)}=Ov_i$; and $U_\pi$ then moves that factor to slot $\pi(1)=i$, leaving every other factor in its original slot, so $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Ov_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$. If $\pi'$ is another permutation with $\pi'(1)=i$, then $\tau:=\pi^{-1}\pi'$ fixes $1$ and $U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*$ agrees with $A_1$ on elementary tensors by [F1], [F3], hence equals it by [F8]; thus $U_{\pi'}A_1U_{\pi'}^*=U_\pi U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*U_\pi^*=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*$ and $O^{(i)}$ is well defined, with the displayed elementary-tensor action. For $\tau\in S_n$ one then has $U_\tau O^{(i)}U_\tau^*=U_{\tau\pi}A_1U_{\tau\pi}^*=O^{(\tau(i))}$, and summing over $i$ with $\tau$ permuting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ gives $U_\tau\Sigma(O)U_\tau^*=\Sigma(O)$ for $\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^nO^{(i)}$; equivalently $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with every $U_\tau$. Since $P_\sigma^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)U_\pi$ is a finite linear combination of the $U_\pi$ by [F4], $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, so it preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and its orthogonal complement and $\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}$; this proves (a) and (c). [F1, F3, F4, F8, F9, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 [Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] By steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], for $\pi(1)=i$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$. Set $R_n:=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, an endomorphism of $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$. Its partial trace $\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}R_n$ is an endomorphism of $H$ by [F5]. Step 1.2 and [F5], [F7] give $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}(R_n(O\otimes I))=n\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)$, proving (d). Unitary transport by $J_n$ preserves positivity and trace, so $R_n$ is positive of trace one; [F5] then makes $\gamma$ positive of trace one and hence a density operator on $H$ by [F6]. For the retained slot $i$, use $J_nU_\pi^*$ as the parenthesisation map; its transported state is $J_nU_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi J_n^{-1}=R_n$ by step 1.3, so its partial trace is the same $\gamma$. More generally the pairing $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))$ for every $O$ uniquely determines $\gamma$: testing against $O=T_{u,v}$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ by [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] clause (e), which determines every matrix entry. For $n=1$, $J_1u=u\otimes1$, $P_\sigma^{(1)}=I$ and $\Sigma(O)=O$, so this pairing gives $\gamma=\rho$. This proves (e), including the one-particle boundary. [F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 [Conclusion and scope] Step 1.1 proves (b), step 2.1 proves (a) and (c), and step 3.1 proves (d) and (e); every argument used only the finite-dimensional tensor construction, the permutation sectors, the partial trace and the trace axioms, and no physical object, preparation or measurement entered, which is clause (f). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Reading of the identities.** The law $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=n\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)$ says that the mean of the sum of one-body slot operators in the sector preparation is $n$ times the trace pairing of a single one-particle operator with a reduced operator $\gamma$ on the one-particle space. Only the identity is asserted here; its physical reading requires the framework postulates and a declared preparation, and is stated separately.
- **Why the factor $n$ appears.** The sum $\Sigma(O)$ has $n$ slot terms with equal pairings by permutation invariance of the sector state, and $\gamma$ is normalised once, $\operatorname{tr}\gamma=1$; the factor $n$ is the multiplicity of the sum, not a further normalisation.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of the endomorphism $T$** by $$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$ This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When $V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map $\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear: $$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$ If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and $BA$ are trace class and $$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let $Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that $$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$ and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if $$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$ for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**. Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The **operator norm** of $T$ is $$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$ The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice principle is used for this assertion. The same number is the least bound of $T$: $$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$ If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives $$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$ When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$, so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such that $$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$ Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

derivations.claim: [The parenthesisation isometry] The map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]

[The first-slot operator] By [F3] the operator $O\otimes I_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)})$ is bounded with $(O\otimes I)(u\otimes w)=Ou\otimes w$. Transporting it through the isometry $J_n$ of clause (b) gives a bounded operator $A_1:=J_n^{-1}(O\otimes I)J_n$ on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $A_1(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=J_n^{-1}(Ov_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=Ov_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for all $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$. [F1, F3, algebra]

[The zero extension and its symmetry] Regard $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and put $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$, an endomorphism of $H^{\otimes n}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is $\rho$ and which vanishes on the orthogonal complement; then $\widetilde\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F6] and [F7], so $\widetilde\rho$ is a density operator on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$. Since $U_\pi$ preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and acts on it as the scalar $\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)$ by [F4], $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

[Slot operators and the permutation invariance of their sum] Fix $i$, choose $\pi\in S_n$ with $\pi(1)=i$ and set $O^{(i)}:=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$; [F9] and step 1.2 give $\|O^{(i)}\|=\|O\otimes I\|\le\|O\|$, and [F3], [F4] give $(O^{(i)})^*=U_\pi(O^*\otimes I)U_\pi^*=(O^*)^{(i)}$, so $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$. On elementary tensors, [F4] gives $U_\pi^*(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi(n)}$; step 1.2 replaces the first factor by $Ov_{\pi(1)}=Ov_i$; and $U_\pi$ then moves that factor to slot $\pi(1)=i$, leaving every other factor in its original slot, so $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Ov_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$. If $\pi'$ is another permutation with $\pi'(1)=i$, then $\tau:=\pi^{-1}\pi'$ fixes $1$ and $U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*$ agrees with $A_1$ on elementary tensors by [F1], [F3], hence equals it by [F8]; thus $U_{\pi'}A_1U_{\pi'}^*=U_\pi U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*U_\pi^*=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*$ and $O^{(i)}$ is well defined, with the displayed elementary-tensor action. For $\tau\in S_n$ one then has $U_\tau O^{(i)}U_\tau^*=U_{\tau\pi}A_1U_{\tau\pi}^*=O^{(\tau(i))}$, and summing over $i$ with $\tau$ permuting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ gives $U_\tau\Sigma(O)U_\tau^*=\Sigma(O)$ for $\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^nO^{(i)}$; equivalently $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with every $U_\tau$. Since $P_\sigma^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)U_\pi$ is a finite linear combination of the $U_\pi$ by [F4], $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, so it preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and its orthogonal complement and $\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}$; this proves (a) and (c). [F1, F3, F4, F8, F9, step 1.2, algebra]

[Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] Fix $i$ and $\pi$ with $\pi(1)=i$; by steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*)=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$, where the middle equality is cyclicity and the last uses $U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi=\widetilde\rho$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\,\Sigma(O))=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}((O\otimes I)J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})=n\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1})O)$ by [F7], [F5] and the explicit form of $A_1$ in step 1.2; with the definition of $\gamma$ this is (d). By [F5] clause (b) applied with $R=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, which is positive of trace one by step 1.3, the operator $\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$ is positive of trace one, so its conjugate $\gamma$ is a density operator on $H$. If instead another named slot is retained, the same computation with the corresponding slot operator produces $\gamma'$ with $n\operatorname{tr}((\gamma'-\gamma)O)=0$ for every $O\in\mathcal B(H)$, hence $\gamma'=\gamma$ on testing against the rank-one operators $O=T_{u,v}$, for which $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]); this proves (e) as well. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

[Conclusion and scope] Step 1.1 proves (b), step 2.1 proves (a) and (c), and step 3.1 proves (d) and (e); every argument used only the finite-dimensional tensor construction, the permutation sectors, the partial trace and the trace axioms, and no physical object, preparation or measurement entered, which is clause (f). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

boundaries.reason: The Hilbert space H is finite-dimensional of dimension d>=1 and n>=1, so the sector space and the tensor powers are nonzero by hypothesis; no empty-index case arises.

boundaries.evidence: O=0 gives every slot operator O^{(i)}=0, hence Sigma(O)=0 and the identity tr(rho Sigma(O))=n tr(gamma 0)=0 is trivial; step 1.3-2.1 covers it as the O=0 instance.
n=1: there is one slot, Sigma(O)=O, and gamma equals rho regarded on K with partial trace over no factors; the trace law reads tr(rho O)=1 tr(gamma O), which is step 2.2 with J_1 the identity.
No diagonalisation of rho is used anywhere; degenerate eigenvalues and coinciding sector projections (n=1) are immaterial, and step 2.1 divides only by n! and never by an eigenvalue.

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. (d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

[The first-slot operator] By [F3] the operator $O\otimes I_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)})$ is bounded with $(O\otimes I)(u\otimes w)=Ou\otimes w$. [The zero extension and its symmetry] Regard $\rho$ as an endomorphism of $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and put $\widetilde\rho:=P_\sigma^{(n)}\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$, an endomorphism of $H^{\otimes n}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ is $\rho$ and which vanishes on the orthogonal complement; then $\widetilde\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F6] and [F7], so $\widetilde\rho$ is a density operator on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$. Since $U_\pi$ preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and acts on it as the scalar $\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)$ by [F4], $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. [F4, F6, F7, algebra]

[Slot operators and the permutation invariance of their sum] Fix $i$, choose $\pi\in S_n$ with $\pi(1)=i$ and set $O^{(i)}:=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$; [F9] and step 1.2 give $\|O^{(i)}\|=\|O\otimes I\|\le\|O\|$, and [F3], [F4] give $(O^{(i)})^*=U_\pi(O^*\otimes I)U_\pi^*=(O^*)^{(i)}$, so $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$. Write $$Z:=\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \rho_\beta:=\frac1Z\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}T_{v_j,v_j},$$ where $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of density operators on $\mathfrak H$, i.e. positive self-adjoint trace-class operators $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]), and for $\rho\in\mathcal D$ with eigenvalues $w_1,\dots,w_d\ge0$ (counted with multiplicity and in any order) define the entropy $$s(\rho):=-\sum_{i:\,w_i>0}w_i\log w_i\in[0,\log d]$$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]]). $$w(\xi)=4\pi^2a|\xi|^2,\qquad K=\mathcal F_2^{-1}M_w\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(K)=\{u:w\mathcal F_2u\in\mathcal H\}.$$

$$H=K+M_V=-a\Delta+V,\qquad D(H)=Y,$$

[F2] For a densely defined operator, the adjoint domain consists of vectors admitting a representing vector in its pairing identity; a symmetric operator is self-adjoint exactly when its adjoint has the same domain and action ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). ## Proof

It is symmetric because $b$ is real and the pairings are integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. If $g\in D(M_b^*)$ with representing vector $h$, every $f\in\mathcal H$ supported on $E_L=\{|b|\le L\}$ belongs to the multiplier domain and satisfies $\langle f,bg-h\rangle=0$ on that set. The vector $\mathbf1_{E_L}(bg-h)$ lies in $\mathcal H$, so testing with that vector proves $h=bg$ a.e. on $E_L$. Increasing the integer $L$ covers the space up to null sets, proving $bg=h\in\mathcal H$ and $g\in D(M_b)$. Conversely the symmetry identity gives every vector of $D(M_b)$ in the adjoint domain with adjoint value $bg$. Thus $M_b$ is self-adjoint on the exact maximal domain, including for the weight $w$. This proof is valid for the finite vector-valued space by its component-sum pairing; it makes no arbitrary family of choices. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 [Fourier transfer, exact H² and normalization] Apply the componentwise unitary $\mathcal F_2$ from [F1] to step 1.1 with $b=w$. For a vector $y$ in the adjoint domain of $K$, changing variables $f=\mathcal F_2u$ in its representing functional gives $\mathcal F_2y\in D(M_w^*)=D(M_w)$ with the corresponding adjoint value; the converse follows from symmetry. Moreover $\|\mathcal F_2u\|_2+\|w\mathcal F_2u\|_2$ is equivalent to $\|(1+w)\mathcal F_2u\|_2$ by the triangle inequality and nonnegativity of $w$, and hence to $\|u\|_Y$. 3.1 [Explicit perturbed inverses on the fixed domain] Multiplication by $V$ is bounded and self-adjoint on $\mathcal H$, with norm at most $v$, since $V$ is real and essentially bounded. The bounded operator space is complete, because an operator-norm Cauchy sequence has a bounded pointwise limit on the complete target and the same uniform Cauchy estimate gives operator-norm convergence. Thus $R_H(z)$ exists, maps into $Y$, and its two ordered inverse equations follow from the factorization. Surjectivity of this range onto $Y$ follows from the second inverse equation. Its norm is at most $\mu^{-1}/(1-v/\mu)=(\mu-v)^{-1}$. [step 2.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

4.1 [Self-adjointness without an AC perturbation theorem] Let $y\in D(H^*)$. By step 3.1, $H-i\mu:Y\to\mathcal H$ is onto; solve $(H-i\mu)x=(H^*-i\mu)y$ with its explicit inverse, so $x\in Y$. Symmetry implies $H^*x=Hx$, whence $y-x\in\ker(H^*-i\mu)$. For a densely defined operator with first-linear pairing, this kernel is $\operatorname{ran}(H+i\mu)^\perp$, directly from the adjoint identity. The other inverse from step 3.1 makes that range all of $\mathcal H$, so $y=x\in Y$. Since $H\subseteq H^*$ by symmetry, the adjoint domains and actions are equal, proving self-adjointness on exactly $Y$. Also $\langle Hu,u\rangle=\langle Ku,u\rangle+\int V\|u\|^2\ge-v\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in Y$, proving the claimed lower bound. Only the two explicit imaginary resolvents were used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, algebra]

5.1 [Graph norms, cores and scope] For $u\in Y$, boundedness of $V$ gives $\|Hu\|\le\|Ku\|+v\|u\|$ and $\|Ku\|\le\|Hu\|+v\|u\|$. Thus the graph norms of $H$ and $K$ are equivalent, and step 2.1 identifies both with the Sobolev norm. The finite-component smooth density from [F3] therefore makes $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C^M)$ graph dense in the exact domain of each operator, which is precisely the core claim. Steps 1.1–4.1 supply the self-adjointness, exact differential action, lower bound and explicit inverses. All primitive suppliers used here assume CC; neither an AC multiplier theorem nor Kato–Rellich nor any assertion concerning a singular potential or an arbitrary spin basis was invoked. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

after.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are

after.claim: [Concrete multiplier, including the adjoint domain] For any real finite-valued measurable function $b$ on $\mathbb R^{3N}$, multiplication on $D(M_b)=\{f:bf\in\mathcal H\}$ is densely defined: $f_L=\mathbf1_{|b|\le L}f$ belongs to this domain and tends to $f$ by dominated convergence. It is symmetric because $b$ is real and the pairings are integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. If $g\in D(M_b^*)$ with representing vector $h$, every $f\in\mathcal H$ supported on $E_L=\{|b|\le L\}$ belongs to the multiplier domain and satisfies $\langle f,bg-h\rangle=0$ on that set. The vector $\mathbf1_{E_L}(bg-h)$ lies in $\mathcal H$, so testing with that vector proves $h=bg$ a.e. on $E_L$. Increasing the integer $L$ covers the space up to null sets, proving $bg=h\in\mathcal H$ and $g\in D(M_b)$. Conversely the symmetry identity gives every vector of $D(M_b)$ in the adjoint domain with adjoint value $bg$. Thus $M_b$ is self-adjoint on the exact maximal domain, including for the weight $w$. This proof is valid for the finite vector-valued space by its component-sum pairing; it makes no arbitrary family of choices.

[Fourier transfer, exact H² and normalization] Apply the componentwise unitary $\mathcal F_2$ from [F1] to step 1.1 with $b=w$. For a vector $y$ in the adjoint domain of $K$, changing variables $f=\mathcal F_2u$ in its representing functional gives $\mathcal F_2y\in D(M_w^*)=D(M_w)$ with the corresponding adjoint value; the converse follows from symmetry. Hence $K$ is self-adjoint on $\mathcal F_2^{-1}D(M_w)$. Since $w=4\pi^2a|\xi|^2$ with $a>0$, $1+w$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of $1+|\xi|^2$. For $u\in L^2$, $w\mathcal F_2u\in L^2$ therefore holds exactly when $(1+|\xi|^2)\mathcal F_2u\in L^2$, which is $u\in Y$ by [F1]. Moreover $\|\mathcal F_2u\|_2+\|w\mathcal F_2u\|_2$ is equivalent to $\|(1+w)\mathcal F_2u\|_2$ by the triangle inequality and nonnegativity of $w$, and hence to $\|u\|_Y$. This proves graph-norm equivalence. The weak-derivative multiplier in [F1] gives $\mathcal F_2(-a\Delta u)=4\pi^2a|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2u$, proving the exact differential action for all $u\in Y$. Finally $\langle Ku,u\rangle=\int w\|\mathcal F_2u\|^2\ge0$, with integrability by Cauchy–Schwarz.

[Explicit perturbed inverses on the fixed domain] Multiplication by $V$ is bounded and self-adjoint on $\mathcal H$, with norm at most $v$, since $V$ is real and essentially bounded. Thus $H=K+M_V$ is symmetric on the dense $Y$ and is closed there: if $u_l\to u$ and $Hu_l\to h$, boundedness gives $Ku_l\to h-M_Vu$, and closedness of $K$ gives $u\in Y$ with $Hu=h$. For $z=\pm i\mu$, the concrete multiplier $(w-z)^{-1}$ is bounded by $\mu^{-1}$ and $|w/(w-z)|\le1$. Therefore $R_0(z)$ maps $\mathcal H$ into $Y$ and satisfies both inverse equations of $K-z$, with range exactly $Y$. On $Y$ the correctly ordered factorization is $H-z=(I+M_VR_0(z))(K-z)$. Since $\|M_VR_0(z)\|\le v/\mu<1$, the geometric series in the statement is the inverse of the first factor: finite-sum multiplication leaves a remainder tending to zero in norm. The bounded operator space is complete, because an operator-norm Cauchy sequence has a bounded pointwise limit on the complete target and the same uniform Cauchy estimate gives operator-norm convergence. Thus $R_H(z)$ exists, maps into $Y$, and its two ordered inverse equations follow from the factorization. Surjectivity of this range onto $Y$ follows from the second inverse equation. Its norm is at most $\mu^{-1}/(1-v/\mu)=(\mu-v)^{-1}$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $N,r\ge1$ be integers, $H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^r)$, $\mathcal S_N=(\mathbb C^r)^{\otimes N}$, and $M=r^N$. In the product basis $e_a=e_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{a_N}$ indexed by $a\in\{1,\dots,r\}^N$, identify $\mathcal S_N$ with $\mathbb C^M$ and write $\mathcal L_N=L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C^M)$. Then:

(a) There is a unique unitary $\Theta_N:H^{\otimes N}\to\mathcal L_N$ such that
$$[\Theta_N(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_N)]_a(x_1,\dots,x_N)=\prod_{j=1}^N[f_j(x_j)]_{a_j}.$$

(b) For $\pi\in S_N$, let $U_\pi$ be the permutation of the complete one-particle factors and $R_\pi e_a=e_{a_{\pi^{-1}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{a_{\pi^{-1}(N)}}$ the permutation of spin factors. With $X^\pi=(x_{\pi(1)},\dots,x_{\pi(N)})$, the conjugate permutation is
$$\mathcal U_\pi:=\Theta_NU_\pi\Theta_N^{-1},\qquad (\mathcal U_\pi\Psi)(X)=R_\pi\Psi(X^\pi).$$
In particular $[\mathcal U_\pi\Psi]_a(X)=\Psi_{(a_{\pi(1)},\dots,a_{\pi(N)})}(X^\pi)$; averaging this combined action gives $\mathcal P_\pm=\Theta_NP_\pm^{(N)}\Theta_N^{-1}$.

(c) The component domain $\mathcal D_N=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C^M)$ is the set of tuples with every scalar component in $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$. If a scalar self-adjoint $T$ has this scalar domain and its domain is preserved by every spatial block permutation, commuting with that permutation on the domain, its finite direct sum $T_M\Psi=(T\Psi_a)_a$ on $\mathcal D_N$ is self-adjoint, retains every scalar lower bound $T\ge cI$, and commutes with the combined permutations on that domain. The restrictions of $T_M$ to $\operatorname{ran}\mathcal P_\pm$, with domain $\mathcal D_N\cap\operatorname{ran}\mathcal P_\pm$, are self-adjoint when the sector is nonzero; on the zero sector the unique zero operator has domain $\{0\}$.

(d) For matrices $A_j\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^r)$, the constant spin action $A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_N$ preserves $\mathcal D_N$ and commutes with $T_M$. Its permutation covariance is
$$R_\pi(A_1\otimes\cdots\otimes A_N)R_\pi^{-1}=A_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes A_{\pi^{-1}(N)}.$$
Thus a common internal unitary $A^{\otimes N}$ commutes with $\mathcal U_\pi$, preserves both sectors and commutes with their restricted operators. This is a tensor identity and asserts no physical spin-statistics assignment. For $r=1$ all spin actions are scalar and $\Theta_N$ is the iterated scalar product unitary; for $N=1$ it is the identity component identification.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N,r,H,\mathcal S_N,M,\mathcal L_N$, the product spin basis, and in (c) the scalar self-adjoint $T$ with domain $W^{2,2}$ and spatial permutation invariance.

[F1] The scalar Euclidean product map is unitary and permits finite component sums ([[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]] Statement); iterating it gives the scalar N-factor product map. The component identification is unitary for every Euclidean dimension and finite component count ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] (a), (b)).

[F2] Tensor pairings multiply, elementary tensors span densely, and spin product bases are orthonormal; bounded factor maps extend with their tensor action and adjoints ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]). Factor permutations and their symmetric/sign averages are unitary and orthogonal projections respectively ([[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] (a)-(c)).

[F3] A self-adjoint operator invariant on its domain under a unitary finite-group permutation representation restricts self-adjointly to each nonzero symmetric/sign sector ([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-permutation-restricted-self-adjointness]] (a)-(d)); the scalar-only application (e) is not needed for a spin sector.

## Proof

**Given:** The data of the Statement and [F1]-[F3].

1.1 [Finite component product unitary] Resolve each one-particle vector into its $r$ components by [F1]. On the dense span of vectors $(g_1e_{a_1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(g_Ne_{a_N})$, send this vector to the function $(\prod_jg_j(x_j))e_a$. Inner products of such vectors are the product of the scalar pairings times $\prod_j\delta_{a_jb_j}$ by [F2]; their image pairings have exactly the same value by the iterated scalar unitary [F1]. Linearity therefore gives a well-defined isometry on this dense span. Its image is dense: in each of the finitely many components the scalar products span densely by [F1]. The isometry extends to the completion; its range is closed by completeness and dense, hence all of $\mathcal L_N$. Expansion of the finite components gives the formula in (a), and equality on a dense span gives uniqueness. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 [Combined permutation] On the component product vectors of step 1.1, applying $U_\pi$ replaces the factor in slot $j$ by the former factor in slot $\pi^{-1}(j)$. Evaluating the product formula gives $(\mathcal U_\pi\Psi)(X)=R_\pi\Psi(X^\pi)$, including the displayed component-index formula. Both operators are bounded unitaries, so the equality extends by density. Conjugating the finite averages of [F2] gives $\mathcal P_\pm$; this simultaneously permutes spatial blocks and spin slots. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 [Finite component domain and self-adjointness] Since there are finitely many components, the definition of weak derivatives shows $\mathcal D_N=(W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C))^{\oplus M}$: derivative testing and integrability hold componentwise in both directions, and all norms are finite sums. The direct sum $T_M$ is dense and symmetric. A vector $\eta$ lies in $D(T_M^*)$ precisely when testing separately in each component puts $\eta_a\in D(T^*)=D(T)$ for every $a$; conversely these finitely many adjoint values give a vector in $\mathcal L_N$. Thus $D(T_M^*)=\mathcal D_N$ and $T_M^*=T_M$. If $T\ge cI$, summing the scalar quadratic inequalities gives $T_M\ge cI$. The hypothesis on scalar spatial permutations gives domain preservation and commutation for their componentwise action; $R_\pi$ is a constant permutation of finitely many components, so it preserves the domain and commutes with $T_M$ too. Their combined action in step 2.1 has both properties. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 [Sector restrictions] Apply [F3] to the self-adjoint $T_M$ of step 3.1 and the combined representation from step 2.1. It gives reduction and self-adjointness on every nonzero $\operatorname{ran}\mathcal P_\pm$ with exactly the stated intersection domain. If a sector is zero, its Hilbert space and dense operator domain are both $\{0\}$, so its unique operator is its own adjoint. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, algebra]

5.1 [Spin covariance and edge cases] A constant spin matrix makes finite linear combinations of the scalar components, so it preserves $\mathcal D_N$ and commutes with the componentwise scalar $T_M$. On elementary spin tensors the conjugation by $R_\pi$ reorders the matrices to $A_{\pi^{-1}(j)}$ in slot $j$; by linearity this is the displayed covariance on all of $\mathcal S_N$. For a common $A$, the reordering leaves $A^{\otimes N}$ unchanged, so it commutes with each combined permutation and its averages; if $A$ is unitary the inverse has the same properties, proving onto preservation of both sectors and their domains. At $r=1$ the sole component is scalar, and at $N=1$ the product formula is the original vector-valued function. These establish (d) and all stated branches. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$ and identify $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$ with Lebesgue measure ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a)$, $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b)$. Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix integers
$d\ge1$ and $r\ge1$, let $H:=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with the Euclidean
integral pairing ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]), let
$$H^{(r)}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr),\qquad \langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}(x)\overline{g_{l}(x)}\,dx,$$
and let $\mathbb C^{r}$ carry the standard inner product with orthonormal basis
$e_{1},\dots,e_{r}$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
Write $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ for the completed tensor product of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] with inclusion $\kappa$.
Then:

(a) the map
$$\Psi_{0}\Bigl((f_{l})\Bigr):=\bigl(x\mapsto(f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{r}(x))\bigr)$$
is a well-defined unitary isomorphism $\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}H\to H^{(r)}$, and
$$\|\Psi_{0}(f)\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|f_{l}\|_{H}^{2},\qquad \langle\Psi_{0}(f),\Psi_{0}(g)\rangle=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\langle f_{l},g_{l}\rangle_{H};$$

(b) the assignment on elementary tensors
$\Theta_{0}(\kappa(u\otimes e_{l})):=\iota_{l}(u)$, where $\iota_{l}(u)$ is
the $r$-tuple with $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ elsewhere, extends uniquely to a
surjective linear isometry $\Theta:H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$
(so $\Theta$ is unitary), and
$\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))=\sum_{l=1}^{r}z_{l}\,\iota_{l}(u)$ for all
$u\in H$, $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}\in\mathbb C^{r}$;

(c) for every $a\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb R^{d})$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^{d}$ one
has the intertwining identities
$$\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\cdot\Theta(w)\bigr)=(M_{a}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w,\qquad \Theta^{-1}\bigl(T_{v}^{(r)}\Theta(w)\bigr)=(T_{v}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w\qquad(w\in H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}),$$
where $M_{a}$ is multiplication by $a$, $T_{v}$ is the Euclidean translation
$T_{v}h:=h(\cdot-v)$ of [[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]]
clause (c), $T_{v}^{(r)}$ is its componentwise action on $H^{(r)}$, and the
bounded amplifications are those of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$ write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are not pairwise distinct in the sense that $v_i=v_j$ for some $i\ne j$, then $P_-(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=0$; in particular, for $n\ge2$, $P_-(u\otimes u\otimes w_3\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=0$ for all $u,w_k\in H$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathfrak H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $H$ be a self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak H$ ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]),
let $N\ge1$, and let $(U_\pi)_{\pi\in S_N}$ be unitary operators on $\mathfrak H$
with $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$ and $U_\pi^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$ for all
$\pi,\sigma\in S_N$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]). Define
$$P_+:=\frac1{N!}\sum_{\pi\in S_N}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{N!}\sum_{\pi\in S_N}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi .$$
Assume that for every $\pi\in S_N$,
$$U_\pi D(H)\subseteq D(H)\qquad\text{and}\qquad U_\pi H\psi=HU_\pi\psi\quad(\psi\in D(H)).$$
Then:

(a) $P_+$ and $P_-$ are orthogonal projections on $\mathfrak H$;

(b) for every $z\in\rho(H)$ one has
$U_\pi(H-z)^{-1}=(H-z)^{-1}U_\pi$ and hence $P_\pm(H-z)^{-1}=(H-z)^{-1}P_\pm$;

(c) $P_\pm D(H)\subseteq D(H)$ and $HP_\pm\psi=P_\pm H\psi$ for every
$\psi\in D(H)$;

(d) if $\operatorname{ran}P_\pm\ne\{0\}$, then the restriction
$H_\pm:=H|_{D(H)\cap\operatorname{ran}P_\pm}$ is a self-adjoint operator on the
Hilbert space $\operatorname{ran}P_\pm$
([[thm-self-adjointness-range-criterion]]);

(e) *application*: let $N\ge1$, $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, let $r\ge1$, let
$V_{\mathrm{ext}},W:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and bounded, put
$V(X):=\sum_{i=1}^NV_{\mathrm{ext}}(x_i)+\sum_{i<j}W(x_i-x_j)$ on
$\mathbb R^{3N}$, let $K$ be the free kinetic operator of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] with all masses
$m_i=m$, let $\Theta:L^2(\mathbb R^3)^{\otimes N}\to L^2(\mathbb R^{3N})$ be
the iterated Euclidean product unitary
([[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), let $U_\pi$ be the
permutation unitaries of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]
and set
$$U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\Theta\,U_\pi\,\Theta^{-1},\qquad P_\pm^{\mathrm{phys}}:=\Theta\,P_\pm^{(N)}\,\Theta^{-1}.$$
Then $H:=K+M_V$ satisfies the hypotheses above for the representation
$U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}$, so $P_\pm^{\mathrm{phys}}$ reduce $H$ and the
restrictions of $H$ to the symmetric and antisymmetric sectors are self-adjoint
on those sectors.

No spin-statistics statement, no identification of a physical species with a
sector, and no claim about bound states or spectra is made.

after.claim: [Finite component product unitary] Resolve each one-particle vector into its $r$ components by [F1]. On the dense span of vectors $(g_1e_{a_1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(g_Ne_{a_N})$, send this vector to the function $(\prod_jg_j(x_j))e_a$. Inner products of such vectors are the product of the scalar pairings times $\prod_j\delta_{a_jb_j}$ by [F2]; their image pairings have exactly the same value by the iterated scalar unitary [F1]. Linearity therefore gives a well-defined isometry on this dense span. Its image is dense: in each of the finitely many components the scalar products span densely by [F1]. The isometry extends to the completion; its range is closed by completeness and dense, hence all of $\mathcal L_N$. Expansion of the finite components gives the formula in (a), and equality on a dense span gives uniqueness.

[Combined permutation] On the component product vectors of step 1.1, applying $U_\pi$ replaces the factor in slot $j$ by the former factor in slot $\pi^{-1}(j)$. Evaluating the product formula gives $(\mathcal U_\pi\Psi)(X)=R_\pi\Psi(X^\pi)$, including the displayed component-index formula. Both operators are bounded unitaries, so the equality extends by density. Conjugating the finite averages of [F2] gives $\mathcal P_\pm$; this simultaneously permutes spatial blocks and spin slots.

[Finite component domain and self-adjointness] Since there are finitely many components, the definition of weak derivatives shows $\mathcal D_N=(W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C))^{\oplus M}$: derivative testing and integrability hold componentwise in both directions, and all norms are finite sums. The direct sum $T_M$ is dense and symmetric. A vector $\eta$ lies in $D(T_M^*)$ precisely when testing separately in each component puts $\eta_a\in D(T^*)=D(T)$ for every $a$; conversely these finitely many adjoint values give a vector in $\mathcal L_N$. Thus $D(T_M^*)=\mathcal D_N$ and $T_M^*=T_M$. If $T\ge cI$, summing the scalar quadratic inequalities gives $T_M\ge cI$. The hypothesis on scalar spatial permutations gives domain preservation and commutation for their componentwise action; $R_\pi$ is a constant permutation of finitely many components, so it preserves the domain and commutes with $T_M$ too. Their combined action in step 2.1 has both properties.

[Sector restrictions] Apply [F3] to the self-adjoint $T_M$ of step 3.1 and the combined representation from step 2.1. It gives reduction and self-adjointness on every nonzero $\operatorname{ran}\mathcal P_\pm$ with exactly the stated intersection domain. If a sector is zero, its Hilbert space and dense operator domain are both $\{0\}$, so its unique operator is its own adjoint.

[Spin covariance and edge cases] A constant spin matrix makes finite linear combinations of the scalar components, so it preserves $\mathcal D_N$ and commutes with the componentwise scalar $T_M$. On elementary spin tensors the conjugation by $R_\pi$ reorders the matrices to $A_{\pi^{-1}(j)}$ in slot $j$; by linearity this is the displayed covariance on all of $\mathcal S_N$. For a common $A$, the reordering leaves $A^{\otimes N}$ unchanged, so it commutes with each combined permutation and its averages; if $A$ is unitary the inverse has the same properties, proving onto preservation of both sectors and their domains. At $r=1$ the sole component is scalar, and at $N=1$ the product formula is the original vector-valued function. These establish (d) and all stated branches.

statement.before:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with a supplied countably infinite orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\ge1}$, let $N\ge1$ be an integer, and let $\varepsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ with $\varepsilon_j\ge b$ for a fixed $b\in\mathbb R$. Use the completed tensor power and permutation-sector projections of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]], and write $\mathfrak H_N^\sigma:=\operatorname{ran}P_\sigma^{(N)}$ for $\sigma\in\{+,-\}$. Then:

(a) For every finitely supported sequence $n=(n_j)_{j\ge1}$ of nonnegative integers with $\sum_jn_j=N$, put $\operatorname{orb}(n):=\{(i_1,\ldots,i_N):\#\{k:i_k=j\}=n_j\text{ for every }j\}$ and
$$b_n^+:=|\operatorname{orb}(n)|^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in\operatorname{orb}(n)}e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_N}.$$
For every $N$-element subset $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_N\}$ of the positive integers, put
$$b_J^-:=\frac1{\sqrt{N!}}\sum_{\pi\in S_N}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)e_{j_{\pi(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\pi(N)}}.$$
These are orthonormal bases of the symmetric and antisymmetric sectors respectively. Denote their countable index sets by $\mathcal C_N^+$ and $\mathcal C_N^-$, and write $b_c^\sigma$ for the corresponding vector. Define $E_n:=\sum_jn_j\varepsilon_j$ and $E_J:=\sum_{j\in J}\varepsilon_j$.

(b) The fixed-$N$ free energy operator is the self-adjoint diagonal operator
$$D(H_N^\sigma):=\left\{\psi=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_N^\sigma}a_cb_c^\sigma:\sum_c|E_c|^2|a_c|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad H_N^\sigma\psi:=\sum_cE_ca_cb_c^\sigma.$$
It is bounded below by $Nb$, and is the closure of its action on finite occupation sums. On elementary tensors of modes it agrees with the restriction of the labelled energy sum $\sum_{k=1}^N\varepsilon_{i_k}$, with the same diagonal-domain closure. Its spectral PVM is
$$E_N^\sigma(B)\psi=\sum_c\mathbf1_B(E_c)a_cb_c^\sigma.$$

(c) For $\beta>0$, let $q_j:=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}>0$, so $q_j\le e^{-\beta b}$. Define the extended positive trace of a bounded positive operator as its nonnegative diagonal sum in the supplied occupation basis; its independence of any other supplied orthonormal basis is proved below. With this trace (allowed to be $+\infty$),
$$Z_N^+(\beta):=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H_N^+}=h_N(q):=\sum_{1\le i_1\le\cdots\le i_N}q_{i_1}\cdots q_{i_N},$$
$$Z_N^-(\beta):=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H_N^-}=e_N(q):=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_N}q_{i_1}\cdots q_{i_N}.$$
All sums are nonnegative-series sums. For either sign,
$$\left(\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}q_k\right)\sum_{j=N}^\infty q_j\le Z_N^\sigma(\beta)\le\left(\sum_{j=1}^\infty q_j\right)^N.$$
For $N=1$ the product is $1$, the tail starts at $1$, and both partition sums equal $\sum_jq_j$. Consequently, for every fixed $N\ge1$ and either statistics,
$$0<Z_N^\sigma(\beta)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_j e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty.$$
The bounded positive operator $e^{-\beta H_N^\sigma}$ is trace class exactly in this case, and its ordinary trace then equals the displayed occupation sum. This is a fixed-$N$ criterion, not a trace over all particle numbers.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the supplied basis, $N\ge1$, the lower bound $b$, real energies $\varepsilon_j\ge b$, and $\beta>0$ in clause (c).

[F1] Completed tensor products have dense algebraic tensor products and the elementary-tensor inner-product formula; the permutation projections are bounded orthogonal projections acting by finite permutation sums ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]).

[F2] In each finite prefix $H_m:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}$ the Slater vectors indexed by $N$-element subsets form an orthonormal antisymmetric basis, and the orbit sums are a nonzero orthogonal symmetric basis ([[thm-nrqm-identical-particles-occupation-number-basis]] (a)-(c)).

[F3] Cauchy-Schwarz controls square-summable coefficient pairings ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]). A complete orthonormal family gives Parseval and norm-convergent coordinate expansion ([[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]). The adjoint of a densely defined operator is characterized by $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$, and equality with the adjoint means self-adjointness ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

[F4] A PVM is strongly countably additive; integration of bounded Borel functions gives the corresponding bounded operator and its scalar spectral integrals ([[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]). The unbounded identity integral has the scalar squared-moment domain and is obtained by bounded coordinate truncations ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]]).

[F5] Finite-rank operators are compact and their operator-norm limits are compact ([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]], [[thm-norm-limit-of-compact-operators-is-compact]]). An absolutely summable nuclear series defines a trace-class operator, with trace equal to the sum of its rank-one traces; a trace-class operator has an absolutely summable diagonal in every supplied orthonormal basis ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; exhaust the supplied basis by finite prefixes, compute the unbounded diagonal adjoint on coordinates, and compare nonnegative fixed-N occupation sums.

**Given:** The data of the statement and [F1]-[F5].

1.1 [Product basis and finite-prefix exhaustion] The tensors $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_N}$ are orthonormal by [F1]. Their span is dense: approximate each factor of an elementary tensor by its finite basis truncation using [F3]; the tensor norm formula and the telescoping difference of two products show convergence of these approximations, and finite sums of elementary tensors are dense by [F1]. (b) The fixed-$N$ free energy operator is the self-adjoint diagonal operator

The bounded positive operator $e^{-\beta H_N^\sigma}$ is trace class exactly in this case, and its ordinary trace then equals the displayed occupation sum. This is a fixed-$N$ criterion, not a trace over all particle numbers.
